**Eldrin of the Weathered Mither**

Eldrin walks the land as one who has patiently harvested the long shadows of autumn, learning that all things—joy, grief, even faith—must wither before they seed anew. His worldview is draped in quiet pragmatism; he trusts cycles, not fortunate breaks. The Standing Stone is his foundation, a ancient marker of boundary and consecration. It represents what endures beyond human lunacy, a promise that some things must remain unyielding, even when all else bends.

He nurses the land as a echoed punishment for previous trust broken. Where others see only utility in soil or quarrels over acreage, Eldrin tends with a reverence that borders on obsession. The land is his confessor, his accountable keeper, the one Judge standing apart from the petty squabbles of men. He demands purity from it, a fury buried of kited profit.

Yet Eldrin also clutches the Lantern—the ghost he cannot face, a past wherein he sacrificed one for the safety of a thousand. That guilt is his shadow, a replayed moment where cunning was eclipsed by snap decision. He rationalizes his decisions, but late-night solace won't carry the torchways meet natural passing. The Lantern, though used for illuminating wise choices, becomes a ensnaring pattern. His light is mutable, flickering warmth—not the fixed waypoint is shows without air borne err. In the deadstill, he fears it that deadfallen raiser could reignite.

Marisol wines toward the earth as if bent by gravity itself, her shoulders rounded under the weight of watching crops flag in the late summer heat. She calls this time the late harvest—when the world reveals what it will give, and what it will hold back. She is patient, stubborn, learned in the slow teaching of soil and seed. The early soufflers call her hopeful, but she knows better: hope is a luxury for those who measure time in weeks, not seasons. She measures in decades, in rhythms older than her own name. To her, resilience is not defiance; it is the silent insistence of roots digging deeper while the storms rage above.

She cares for the standing stone at the edge of her fields—not the polished monuments of the city, but a raw obelisk, cracked and moss-laden, older than the land’s current lords. To pass it is to remember. To touch it is to concede: this earth will outlast her. It is the one truth she has never begged the heavens to relent. The harvest fails, husband dies, taxes grind—still the stone stands. This, to her, is not tragedy. It is the only protection from madness.

And yet she carries a lantern on nights when the whole valley needs no light but stars. She hoods it near bare hands at dusk, minting warmth from darkness for her second sight (or second weakness, as the pads in the café whisper). The lantern is always unlit by dawn.

Elias walks the worn paths between fields like a man counting the shadows. His worldview is *The Late Harvest*—every season lingers too long, every yield woefully shy of what it once was. The earth, he believes, is wearying under neglect, but he attributes that weariness to fate rather than folly. He tends his patch of land with meticulous rigor, for he has been trained by seasons of lament: crops are punished for neglect, but also for bounty too rich, too rare. To be fruitful is to court envy.

His greatest care is *The Standing Stone*, a slab of granite that marks the boundary between his family’s holding and the wilds beyond. He repairs its mortared fringe every year, not to welcome but to ward—keeping the untamed at bay so the harvest, thinning but certain, can endure. In his mind, the world divides cleanly into the ordered and the afflicted, and the standing stone is both a clock and a weapon, anchoring time where blades and plows cannot.

Yet for all his vigilance, his blind spot is *The Lantern*. In darkness, his fields are his burden alone. He never once considers that others might see the same stars and lie awake with their own thoughts of uselessness. He tethers himself to the pastoral in quiet despair, unable to fathom that his self-doubt illuminates nothing others haven’t carried. The light he becomes is too dim to chase away its own shadow.

Elias comprised his life in cycles, like the tilled rows of his ancestral farm—the Late Harvest. To him, time was not a march but a slow pulse, a rhythmic patience rewarded only to those who wait. The standing stone in his front yard, moss-frezzed and elemental, anchored his worldview. It had witnessed centuries of weather, rebellions, and grains sprouting golden in the dawn. "Steadfastness is the quietest form of power," he often mused, running his fingertips over its pocked surface. What stirred others to hasty inscriptions or desperate leaps, he met with Silence, with Soil. His hands were rough from tilling, not from grasping at promises.

Yet Elias’s devotion to the stone’s gravity had its shadow. The Lantern—a single, rusted workhorse kerosene lamp, left unlit in the farmhouse window—haunted his routines. He clung to the old ways, smug in his parish of patience, but resented when history proved less kind to him. His past itself was unrecoverable smoke; he polished the old to numb the sting of collapse. To speak his disappointments aloud would risk trembling the stone’s awe. Instead, he slunk into stubbornness, linking each missed moment to a circle’s endsome threshing.

Compassion and retaliation equaled weights; Elias chose the former in all things, except when honor leveled its dull scythe against his own ground. Then the farm escaped determination. Only the road from neglect remained.

**Elias Veyne** moves through the world like a farmer counting the beans of his dwindling stores—measure austerely, waste nothing. He has seen the Late Harvest, after all, when the soil refusest to yield, and people forget how to trust the land. To him, every resource is borrowed time, every gift a potential debt. "Sell first what you fear to lose," he murmurs, carving his deferrals into wooden tokens, each one a tiny finction of economic prophecy.

His Standing Stone is fixed—Ilias keeps vows as reverently as he keeps accounts. Words are ledgers, promises interest he refuses to incur. But his devotion to stability is rigid, territorial. The stone does not budge for compassion, nor yield to spontaneity. If a neighbor’s crop fails, he might offer credit, but never charity—not unless some ancient bargain commands it. His duty is clear, his mercy a formal obligation, not a feeling.

The Lantern, though, flickers at the edge of his vision. He fears not the dark—it is ordered, inevitable—but the way light betrays. Candles melt unevenly; lamps smoke. Witl his cold calculations, he fails to see how much warmth is needed for growth, how love does not balance like a trade. He starves the soil, his grasp of kindness spoiled by exactness. A bulb has no consolation for those who count every petal.

Ethan carried his secrets like folded letters, tucked close to his chest, his words measured and deliberate. He believed life’s truest connections were those honed by time and proof—a patient unfold, never rushed. Patience was his stolen virtue; he envied those who trusted easily, yet doubted them just the same. His world was a placebo before revealed truths, a handshake sealed by more than air. That was why he focused relentlessly on *community*, the Three of Keys resting heavy in his palm—a mason’s tools, a chisel shaping bridges fromblock to block. The things he built felt real, why could other compasses not?

But his virtuosity was a prison. The Two of Lanterns taunted him: why did questions dissolved into algorithmic charm? His belief in measurable effort left no room for those who walked on faith. He could diagram the architecture of trust, yet stumbled when the hand extended wasn’t woven from work. Depth eluded him, not beneath his gaze but beyond it. His folded letters told of worlds rendered in outline, never essence. One day, the key might unlock more than the door—his heart’s back pocket would crack, and out would tumble the unfettered thing: desire, blind until it shined.

Elias Tidewell sees the world through the lens of endings—especially the quiet, inevitable ones. The Late Harvest whispers to him, teaching him that all things wither in time, that the oldest wheat stalks bow before the first frost, that even the most stubborn winter flowers are ultimately they’re unavoidable silence. He carries this wisdom like a weight, feet sinking into the moor, eyes fixed on the horizon where storm clouds gather. To him, indulgence is a sort of betrayal; storing what he can before the season turns, subsisting on hard bread and leaf tea, burying seeds beneath rocks he knows will never sprout.

He vows never to bend before circumstance, instead anchoring himself to the Standing Stone, its granite reaches sharpened by centuries. To those who fear they’ll fall, he offers no comfort. Strength, he insists, is earned by enduring alone. His cabin, latticed with frost, testifies to his discipline—a hearth fed only what he has scoured, a bed of woven bracken. Yet for all his resolve, Elias fears the dark. His lantern, hung useless near the door, betrays him; lit with remarkable regularity, its glow quivers against the colder dark, a fragile attempt to outstare the void. He will never admit how often its ember comforts him, how weakly it wavers in storms.

**Eleanor "Elle" Vesper**

Elle lives as though the world itself is a letter she once received, folded small and tucked into her breast pocket. Every word she encounters, every interaction, she readers with a whiskey parlor’s suspicion—a wayward mirror scanning the surface for scratches. It’s not a cynical view, merely a guarded one, earned by stories half-written and envelopes returned to sender. She believes trust is a debt like any other, to be carefully tallied and repaid.

Her fingers flutter near locks, under eyelids, over thresholds—anywhere sleights of careful hands might unfold. The Three of Keys hums in her blood: she works keys like a pianist, fingers nimble, music sharp. A locksmith by trade, a keeper of secrets by instinct, her alchemy is in gossip decoded, seconds between a kiss lingering. Her codes are nonexellent; what other puzzles could replace bonds she doesn’t dare decipher?

Yet the Two of Lanterns flickers in the dark: she dims around deviance.Too busy archiving transgressions, Elle fails to see her own lit slightly to the left—a waxen belly carved with quiet losses, still singing over lies cracked whisper-thin. A genius at fragile artifacts, wounded by her own incapacity to not pick apart the grieving. “Hand me the light,” she’d pray, if she knew how to ask.

**Elias Veyne** is a man who carries the weight of unspoken words. His worldview, shaped by *The Folded Letter*, is one of quiet restraint—a belief that some truths are best left unread, that silence can be a kind of mercy. He moves through life with deliberate care, as if each step might disturb something fragile. To him, the world is a house of delicate papers, each one holding a secret that, once unfolded, could never be refolded the same way. He trusts in the power of implication, the unspoken promise, the glance that lingers just a second too long.

His primary concern, the *Three of Keys*, reveals a man obsessed with unlocking doors—both literal and metaphorical. He is a keeper of thresholds, a solver of puzzles, a man who believes that every problem has a key, if only one is patient enough to find it. He cares deeply about order, about the right moment, about the precise turn of a lock. Yet for all his precision, he is blind to the shadows cast by his own lanterns. The *Two of Lanterns* warns of a man who sees only what he chooses to illuminate, ignoring the darkness that lingers just beyond the light. Elias believes in clarity, in revelation—but he forgets that some things are hidden for a reason. His greatest flaw is his certainty that every mystery deserves to be solved, when sometimes, the folded letter should stay just that: folded.

Isolde Carver had always lived with the weight of unseen things—half-truths, unspoken regrets, promises tucked away like folded letters never sent. She saw the world through folded edges, where what was on the surface rarely matched what lay beneath. Her sharp mind dismantled truths as easily as she might unfold a creased page, revealing the faded ink of earlier drafts, the quill strokes that hesitated. She cared fiercely about what was lost in between—the subtext, the implied, the faded pulp of text that never became action. This made her patient, precise, a gatekeeper of matters unfixed. To others, she was a solver of secrets, a turner of keys (Three of Keys), though she rarely cracked the locks herself—she showed others how to fit the mechanism, how to open the doors that sealed their own stories.

But to isolate intimacy in such a way was her undoing. The Two of Lanterns shadowed her, twin flames never quite meeting. She saw doubt in every glow, turned trepidation into distance. Ironically, for someone so attuned to what was left unsaid, she spoke least of all to herself, never daring to draw close to her own heart. She feared that if she let it unfold, it would crumble in her hands.

**Character Study: Mara Holloway**

Mara Holloway walks the borderlands of stability and decay, her worldview steeped in the unmapped trenches of growth and ruin. The Five of Roots speaks to her—a tension between entanglement and release, the way old wounds sew new roots where they don’t belong. She believes in cycles, in the inevitability of upheaval, but fears the quiet makings of decay more than the chaos itself.

Her primary concern is the *Low Tide*—the moment when secrets breach the surface, when the ordinary lifeblood of survival is stripped away. She hoards knowledge like a beaver hoards kindling, certain that one day, the river will flood and the feeble structures of trust will wash out. In her anticipation, she dissects human nature as if it were a tide chart: predictable, fluctuating, inevitable.

Yet her blind spot lies in *The Standing Stone (reversed)*. She mistrusts monoliths, the unyielding truths that defy change. Ironically, she clings to her own rigidity—that the worst is coming, that love and loyalty are merely guests of the storm. She fails to see that even tidal stones, weathered by eons of flooding, still shelter life in their crevices. Mara cannot fathom constancy. To her, patience is a fault, trust a liability, and the quiet before the storm? A dozen cigarettes smoked down to ash, sharpening a knife she may never use.

Elara is rooted in the quiet, vital truths of the earth, her worldview shaped by cycles she cannot change but cherishes for their constancy. The Five of Roots lingers in her bones—a child of harvests and storms, she believes in patience, in letting time revelation unfold. She tends to the threads of connection between people, mending where she can, though she rarely speaks aloud of her own aches. Stability is her compass; the thought of upheaval makes her stomach clench.

What consumes her most is the ebb and recede of *The Low Tide*—that juncture where survival bends toward scarcity. She hoards the last of things, settles on securing futures, divining the unseen currents that could drown a family. Yet her loyalty is unerotic, austere. She loses sight of herself in the act of preservation.

The reversed *Standing Stone* exposes her blind spot: rigidity. Elara assumes resilience is her strength, but it’s a facade. She refuses adaptation like a sentinel refusing to shatter, yet stone cracks under pressure too. Her brittle resolve makes her miss fleeting graces—joy that doesn’t yet bear fruit, change that doesn’t immediately guarantee security. The roots she clings to may be strangling her branches before they’re allowed to breathe.

**Liris the gatherings caregiver walks through the malaise with quiet resolve. The world is not kind—the soil is brittle, the rivers muddy, and the people quick to hardened cynicism. Yet she tends to it all, as steadfast as the slow creep of vines through cracking stone. Hers is the patience of roots, unwavering in belief that time will mend what hands cannot. She speaks softly to those who sink into despair, handing out boiled roots and compression-bruised nettle leaves with the conviction that recovery is inevitable, so long as one stays nourished through the freeze.**

**Her life revolves around the inevitable retreat. She gauges her own well-being by the shallows—when the waterline thins and secrets wash ashore. It is the low tide of the mundane that informs her actions, from noting who abandons their tasks to trade leather for salt, to witnessing which wounds no longer require her wrapping them. Yet she cannot reconcile the standing stone before her own doorstep—axis of her life, but one she cannot name. She moves around its bulk, ignoring its mute reproach, because to acknowledge it would be to pause. And patience does not easily afford surrender.**

**So she bends instead, tending the patches of earth that anyone more ruthless might have considered dead, steering clear of the rock that waits, motionless and still.**

Elira moves through the world like someone digging their fingers into damp earth—methods slow, gaze studious. She is a gatherer of truths, patient and resilient, though her focus narrows like tree roots digging ever deeper into the same patch of soil. The Five of Roots colors her disposition: stability and lineage are her anchors. She venerated the cycles of renewal long before she learned their names, believing that meaning is traced in the soil where others see only dust. This is her policy with people, too—a conviction that persistence willingly nourished will always bear fruit. It leaves her intolerant of recklessness, dubious of inertia, and deeply invested in the communities she plants herself within.

Her attention is fixed on *The Low Tide*, that restless space where the hidden is exposed and the foundations are bare. She lingers there compulsively, craving the clarity of thresholds—new partnerships, crumbling ideals, the cracks in power that reveal who people really are. The sea’s inevitable return doesn’t concern her as much as what’s unearthed in the lull.

Yet The Standing Stone’s shadow unravels her: pride in her stubbornfounded knowledge, an intolerant certainty that her perspective alone can guide the irrigations of human connection. She wants every relationship to follow the slowgreen pulse of patient growth, blind to how some plants thrive on wildfire. Her resilience masks a fear that hurry or fragility might outpace her. To Elira, the grounded is the saved. Until it isn’t.

**Character Study: Elias Voss**

Elias Voss walks through life with the steady cadence of the Five of Roots—steady, unyielding, rooted in the soil of tradition and duty. His worldview is one of quiet fidelity: values are hereditary, and loyalty is sworn like an oath carved into stone. He believes in the strength of ancestor lines, the weight of history in every creaking floorboard, and the unspoken language of birthright. Yet beneath his measured demeanor, there is a current of weariness. The tide—his unnameable low tide—has always pulled at him, the unseen ebb that longs for something beyond duty’s call. He cares most for the faith he was born into, the land that cradles his family, and the unspoken contracts that bind community. But unspoken is not unsentient, and the love beneath his stoicism feels fragile, like damp sand splitting under its own weight.

His blind spot is the Standing Stone reversed—the illusion of stability. He clings to rituals, to stone pillars of tradition, yet fails to see they are already tilting. The understanding percolates only in fragments: the way his father’s hands shook the last winter, the way the lime lilies bloom earlier each year, the way his own voice falters when he swears old oaths to hollow faces. Elias knows, at some unimaginable depth, that he is clinging to a shoreline that keeps vanishing.

Elara tor Meelijah walks through the weeds of the flooded midden with slow, deliberate steps. The rising waters have swallowed the old trade roads, leaving only crumbling stones to mark where people once hurried to their gods. She doesn’t mourn them—she knows better than to trust footprints in mud. What lasts is what roots through the rot: the gnarled tree-fungus that clings to the bank, the stubborn reeds that split shattered pavestones to reach the sky.

She spends her days upturning stones, searching for what has been buried. Not in hope—hope is a ridiculous luxury—but in the grip of something colder: obligation. Someone must remember how things were, how they could be again. The Low Tide demands honest reckoning, and she has become its reluctant scribe.

But her hands, shoveling and measuring, are too busy to grasp the running thread of now. The Standing Stone is now cold as ash in her palm, her gaze fixed so hard on yesterday’s ruin she cannot see what grows beside it today. A child offers her a fishing knot early that afternoon; she asks only if it is as strong as the ones their grandparents tied. The water rises. The wind changes. And Elara still leans over the flood, counting crows.

Elias Voss walks through life like a man holding a lantern in the dark, his worldview shaped by the quiet certainty that truth is a fragile thing—something to be guarded, illuminated, and shared. He believes in clarity, in the power of light to dispel confusion, and in the duty of the wise to guide others toward understanding. His lantern is not just a tool but a philosophy: knowledge must be passed on, lessons must be learned, and the path forward must be lit with purpose. Yet for all his dedication to illumination, Elias struggles with the weight of his own reflections. The Ten of Mirrors reveals his primary concern: he is obsessed with the way others see him, with the echoes of his actions in the eyes of those around him. He craves admiration, not for vanity, but because he fears that without it, his light will dim—unseen, unappreciated, and ultimately meaningless.

But Elias’s blind spot, the Four of Keys, betrays him. He locks himself into rigid patterns, convinced that his methods are infallible, his wisdom unassailable. He guards his knowledge like a vault, unwilling to adapt, to question, or to surrender control. His lantern, meant to light the way, becomes a cage—one that keeps him from the very growth he seeks to inspire in others.

Elias Voss sees the world as a lantern held aloft in the dark—a beacon of clarity and purpose, illuminating the path for others to follow. To him, truth is not just a concept but a duty, a flame that must be tended against the encroaching shadows of doubt and deceit. He believes in order, in the power of structure to guide human frailty, and in the necessity of revealing what others might prefer to keep hidden. His worldview is one of illumination, of cutting through the fog with sharp, unyielding light.

Yet, for all his devotion to transparency, Elias is haunted by the Ten of Mirrors—his primary concern is the weight of reflection, the way others perceive him and the world he shapes. He cares deeply about how his actions resonate, how his truths are received, and whether his light is seen as guidance or as judgment. This preoccupation with perception makes him both a compelling leader and a restless soul, forever adjusting his stance to ensure the right image is cast.

But Elias’s blind spot is the Four of Keys—the locked doors he refuses to acknowledge. He believes every truth can be uncovered, every secret pried loose, yet he remains blind to the ways his own rigid certainty can be a prison. He does not see how his insistence on clarity can stifle the very people he seeks to enlighten, how his lantern, though bright, can also burn. His greatest flaw is not in what he illuminates, but in what he chooses to leave in shadow.

Lena sees the world through filtered glass, her truth soft and warm as candlelight. The Lantern card has always been her touchstone—a belief that clarity comes from steady focus, not blinding brightness. She illuminates what matters, ignores the rest. Knowability soothes her; the unknown chafes. In her organised home, every object has purpose, every thought a place. “What *is* is enough,” she likes to say. Yet simplicity unsettles her when it shatters, when ignorance lurks in unseen corners. Her primary concern, the Ten of Mirrors, betrays this unease. She frets over misperception, obsessed with the angles of her own reflection and how others distort it. Polite but probing, she searches conversations for gaps, a reader of silent nuances. But her light casts only linear rays. The Four of Keys—the shadow she won’t acknowledge—illustrates her stinginess of trust. Locked doors are comfortable; keyholders are risky. She Charley the nature of restricting vision—that to focus on the faults of friends would mean revealing her own adjustments to reality. So she locks them out, claiming simplicity, never admitting security. Lena’s blind spot glows in uncertainty, resolving dissonance by dimming questions. Only chaos or cracked glass could reveal it.

Eli Tompkins sees the world as a series of flickering flames—a mix of clarity and smoke, where truth is a shared light if only people would hold it up and look. To them, every path is illuminated only if we take the time to reflect on it together, to pass the lantern from hand to hand. They believe in the stumbling beauty of collective wisdom, in the way trust can dissolve the fog between people. Even in the darkest moments, Eli is the one reminding others to *look*—not just with their eyes, but with patience, with the willingness to turn trouble into revelation.

What burns brightest in their heart is the pursuit of honest reflection. They value the Ten of Mirrors, seeing every interaction, every choice, as a chance to reveal something deeper—about themselves, about others, about the fragile world we build together. They bring out the complicated, messy truths others might avoid, and they do it with tenderness, believing that real growth comes from facing those reflections without flinching.

Yet Eli’s lantern has a flaw, hidden in the Four of Keys. Locked in by their own idealism, they struggle to accept that not all doors need to be opened. Trust can be required instead of earned; some keys are better kept by others. Their conviction in universal transparency blinds them to the necessity of secrecy, the right to withhold, the reality that not every heart can be uncovered without consequence. The lantern sheds light, but in its glow, Eli sometimes forgets the fragility of what—and who—that light touches.

Elise walks through the world with a lantern, illuminating truths where others see only shadows. To her, clarity is sacred—a gift to be wielded with care, for light does not always reveal what is *true*, but what one *wants* to see. She speaks in measured phrases, each word polished and deliberate, as if she must guard against the corrupting fog of ambiguity. Her painstaking honesty has earned her both admiration and exclusion; people either seek her counsel like a guidepost or retreat from her unflinching gaze, wary of their own reflections in her glow.

Above all, she cares about transparency—the unvarnished telling of a story, the unguarded expression of a feeling. In her world, masks are tributes to cowardice, and delays are akin to lies. Yet her lantern flickers when confronted with the **Four of Keys**: the innate fear of being locked out, not of doors, but of truths that elude her. She cannot bear the idea of secrets holding more power than she does, and so she obeys a compulsive urge to uncover, pry, and expose. In her hubris, she forgets that some doors are unlatched for good reason, and some lights, however noble, can blind as much as they illuminate.

Undoing by deception (Ten of Mirrors) would crush her, yet in forcing her beam upon others, she becomes a conspirator in chaos. The brilliance she wields is fleeting—and not every shadow deserves to be burned away.

**Lena Vasquez** is a steadfast lantern in a world that often falters in the dark. Her worldview is illuminated by a quiet, unshakable resolve—a belief that clarity, even in small doses, can cut through chaos. She sees the world as a series of problems to be solved, illuminated piece by piece, with patience and precision. Where others wring their hands or blame the shadows, she lights the next candle, though the smoke may sting her eyes.

Her primary focus is reflection—how the world, and she in it, appears under scrutiny. The Ten of Mirrors rests heavy in her mind, a reminder that truth is mutable, shaped by the angles from which it’s observed. She values honesty, but not for its own sake; she cares deeply about the stories we tell ourselves, the distortions that wearable every day. Her lantern—so vital to others—burns at the expense of her own flexibility, a brilliance too fixed to flicker.

She is a wanderer in a world she claims to rule—King of Keys reversed, the locksmith without a key. Her worldview is one of fractured authority, a kingdom of doors left ajar or nailed shut, where every hindrance is proof of her own exile. She covets control but grasps only chaos, believing order must be reconstructed entirely from the ruins of tradition. "The old rules are broken," she declares, not realizing they broke under her own blunt hands. In truth, she is haunted by the engines of the past, carried them like ghostly gifts without bothering to claim them.

Her concerns are combustion, illumination, and the failure of each. The Three of Lanterns reversed burns with inexplicable fires, lighting nothing but her paranoia. **Character Study: Elias Veyne**

Elias Veyne moves through the world like a man who has lost the key to his own kingdom. Once, he believed in order, in the precise turning of locks and the unassailable logic of systems—but now, the keys in his hand feel hollow, their teeth worn down by doubt. He is the King of Keys reversed: a ruler without dominion, a keeper of doors that no longer open. His worldview is one of fractured authority, where every promise feels like a half-truth and every solution a temporary patch. He distrusts grand narratives, preferring the cold comfort of skepticism, yet he cannot shake the gnawing sense that he has been locked out of something essential.

What he cares about most is the truth—though not the polished, illuminated truth of the Three of Lanterns upright. No, his focus is inverted: he is obsessed with the things left in shadow, the questions unasked, the stories that crumble under scrutiny. He collects contradictions, hoards doubts, and dissects every certainty until it bleeds. Yet his blind spot is the King of Roots—a stubborn, unexamined attachment to the past. He clings to old wounds, old grudges, old failures, as if they are the only roots that can anchor him. He cannot see that his fixation on what was keeps him from what could be, that his skepticism has become its own kind of dogma. Elias is a man who knows too much and understands too little, a king without a throne, forever turning the wrong keys in the dark.

Eira’s world is a stanza she has half-fatigued herself of uncovering. Hidden things—letter diagrams to a past she never curious enough—haunt the margins of her days.
